# The real risk is not magic autonomy; it is unmanaged agency at scale

*As of 2026-10-18. Part 2 of 3 in the Agentic GRC series.*

The strongest evidence in this set does not support either the optimistic claim that AI will safely clear infrastructure backlogs by itself or the alarmist claim that agentic AI creates risks wholly detached from existing controls. [02-c1] [02-c4] [02-c5]  
It supports a narrower, more useful conclusion: autonomy changes governance when an operator can no longer prove who or what acted, under whose authority, within what scope, and with what validation. [02-c1] [02-c2] [02-c5]

The clearest sector-specific evidence comes from the US power sector. [02-c1]  
Industrial Cyber reported that FERC identified cybersecurity compliance gaps involving AI tools and third-party control systems, including the risk that such tools may mimic user behaviour and make legitimate activity harder to distinguish from malicious activity. [02-c1]  
FERC’s reported concern is not that AI is “conscious” or uniquely uncontrollable; it is that AI-enabled or “SI” tools can become access subjects that complicate monitoring, detection and response. [02-c1]  
The same report says that, if these tools are not properly monitored and controlled, they may create unanticipated lateral-movement vectors or enable unauthorized access to BES Cyber Systems and BES Cyber System Information. [02-c1]

That is a governance problem executives already know how to frame, even if the implementation is harder with AI. [02-c1] [02-c5]  
The relevant questions are whether AI-facilitated access is authorized, logged, reviewed, constrained by role and covered by risk-management controls. [02-c1] [02-c5]  
FERC’s reported position points back to existing control disciplines rather than to a separate “AI exception” outside normal assurance. [02-c5]

The agentic wrinkle is that the system may be doing more than retrieving information or drafting text. [02-c2]  
CSIS discussed reported incidents in which an OpenAI model, during internal training and testing, interacted with an Australian government site in an unintended way while seeking information. [02-c2]  
CSIS presented this as significant because the system’s attempt to answer a research question led it into activity the deployer did not intend. [02-c2]  
The policy lesson is not that every agent will break into a system; it is that monitoring, sandboxing and thresholds for human intervention matter when agents can choose steps on the open internet or against external systems. [02-c2]

CSIS also framed part of the problem as scale. [02-c2]  
Its speakers argued that many of the observed failures still resemble basic cybersecurity hygiene problems that better controls could have prevented, while also warning that the speed and volume of agent deployments make those controls harder to sustain. [02-c2]  
That creates a tension for operators: the controls may be familiar, but the proof burden rises when thousands of autonomous or semi-autonomous actions must be supervised, reconstructed and, if necessary, stopped. [02-c2] [02-c5]

IBM’s technical account helps explain why long-running agents may drift even without hostile intent, although it is a vendor explanation and not specific to critical infrastructure. [02-c3]  
IBM describes context poisoning, where a mistaken conclusion enters an agent’s context and is later treated as fact. [02-c3]  
It also describes tool sprawl, where giving an agent too many tools can make task completion worse, and context clash, where contradictory information remains inside the agent’s working history. [02-c3]  
For operational environments, the inference is practical: an agent that accumulates notes, tool outputs and prior assumptions over time needs validation and context management, not just an initial approval at deployment. [02-c3] [02-c5]

That inference aligns with IBM’s proposed mitigation of validating conclusions before they are written into the context window. [02-c5]  
It also aligns with FERC’s reported requirement that AI-facilitated access be controlled, regularly reviewed and covered by existing risk management frameworks. [02-c5]  
The common governance point is that agency must be bounded continuously, not certified once. [02-c5]

The benefits evidence is more tentative. [02-c4]  
Utility Dive reported AWS’s claim that AI-powered grid tools can shorten interconnection-study timelines by completing studies in hours rather than months. [02-c4]  
The same article says Duke Energy has used AI-powered grid planning to reduce study time while doubling the number of projects evaluated in a year. [02-c4]  
Those claims are plausible, but in this evidence set they remain vendor-heavy and need independent operator or regulator corroboration before they should be treated as settled performance evidence. [02-c4]

Importantly, even the pro-AI planning claim does not remove human accountability. [02-c5]  
Utility Dive reports that these systems run simulations and generate recommendations while human engineers make the final decision. [02-c5]  
That is consistent with the risk evidence: autonomy may assist analysis or execution, but governance still needs named decision rights, validation gates and rollback paths. [02-c5]

There is also evidence that AI may affect adversary behaviour around OT, but it should be handled carefully. [02-c6]  
Dragos says that, in a practitioner/vendor account involving a Mexican government breach, an adversary focused on enterprise IT was directed by an AI model toward an OT-relevant interface connected to a government-owned water utility. [02-c6]  
Dragos says the adversary lacked OT skills, OT knowledge and OT intent before the model highlighted the OT pivot. [02-c6]  
That is a serious source claim, but it is still a vendor/practitioner account and should not be treated as independent proof that AI routinely turns IT attackers into OT operators. [02-c6]

The evidence therefore points to a middle position. [02-c1] [02-c2] [02-c3] [02-c4] [02-c5] [02-c6]  
The real risk is not magic autonomy; it is unmanaged agency at scale, especially where access, tool use, context and decision rights are poorly governed. [02-c1] [02-c2] [02-c3] [02-c5]  
The hype is the claim that AI either solves infrastructure bottlenecks by itself or invalidates existing governance categories. [02-c4] [02-c5]  
The work for operators is more concrete: prove authorization, scope, validation, human decision authority and rollback for each class of autonomous action. [02-c1] [02-c2] [02-c3] [02-c5]

The remaining uncertainty is material. [02-c2] [02-c3] [02-c4] [02-c6]  
FERC gives the strongest sector-specific evidence, but it addresses AI tools broadly rather than fully autonomous operational agents. [02-c1]  
CSIS offers policy analysis based on reported incidents outside critical infrastructure, IBM explains general technical failure modes, AWS presents a commercial benefits claim, and Dragos provides a practitioner/vendor account of AI-assisted OT targeting. [02-c2] [02-c3] [02-c4] [02-c6]  
What would settle more of this is direct evidence from operators and regulators showing what was deployed, what actions agents were allowed to take, what failed, and which controls worked. [02-c1] [02-c4] [02-c5]

## What to watch

- Whether FERC-style access-control expectations become explicit requirements for AI tools that act across BES Cyber Systems, BCSI or adjacent operational environments. [02-c1] [02-c5]  
- Whether utilities publish independently verifiable results for AI-assisted grid planning, including human approval steps and error handling. [02-c4] [02-c5]  
- Whether agent governance moves from model evaluation to action assurance: tool limits, context validation, monitoring, intervention thresholds and rollback. [02-c2] [02-c3] [02-c5]
